# A repeatable path to green {#sec-build}

A build should answer one question the same way on every machine: does this change work?
Targets describe the architecture; presets make the answer repeatable.

## Targets carry their own needs {#sec-targets}

A target owns its sources, compile settings, and dependencies. `PUBLIC` means a consumer
needs the dependency to use your headers. `PRIVATE` means only the implementation needs it.
That small rule keeps build dependencies honest.

::: {.snippet source="src/canvas/CMakeLists.txt"}

```cmake
target_link_libraries(app_canvas
    PRIVATE app_controls\n)
```

:::

## Presets name working configurations {#sec-presets}

A preset captures a configuration once. A workflow chains configure, build, and test. Use the
same names locally and in CI, so a green result means the same thing everywhere.

| Preset | What it records |
|---|---|
| Configure | generator, build directory, and cache values |
| Build | which configured build to compile |
| Test | test options and environment |
| Package | how to package the installed files |
| Workflow | a sequence of those steps |

The `dev` workflow configures, builds, and tests. `release` adds packaging; `asan` runs the
tests with sanitizers. Each step can also be run separately when you are iterating.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The dev workflow

The workflow names the configure, build, and test presets it runs, in order:

::: {.snippet source="CMakePresets.json"}

```json
    {\n      "name": "dev",\n      "displayName": "Debug build and all tests",
        { "type": "test", "name": "dev" }\n      ]\n    }
```

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The dev configure preset

The configure preset inherits the shared `base` settings and chooses a Debug build:

::: {.snippet source="CMakePresets.json"}

```json
    { "name": "dev", "inherits": "base", "cacheVariables": { "CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE": "Debug" } }
    { "name": "dev", "inherits": "base", "cacheVariables": { "CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE": "Debug" } }
```

:::

The source links lead to the complete file, including the base, build and test presets and
the sanitizer and release workflows.
:::

```sh
cmake --workflow --preset dev
cmake --workflow --preset asan
cmake --workflow --preset release
```

Put machine-specific Qt locations in the environment. The preset reads `Qt6_ROOT`, which can
point to the installed Qt kit. Keep project choices in presets so CI and the team share them.

## Static and dynamic libraries {#sec-linking}

A static library becomes part of the linked executable. A dynamic library stays separate and
must be available when the application runs. Static linking makes the application independent
of that particular library file, while dynamic linking lets a library be replaced separately.
The choice affects deployment and license obligations. Sketchbook uses dynamic Qt libraries,
so its release package must include the required Qt libraries and plugins.

## Qt's CMake commands {#sec-qt-cmake}

Qt adds CMake commands for the parts of an application that need Qt's build tools. This
**adapted example** brings the main commands together in one file; Sketchbook splits them
between its top-level build and the application and feature folders:

```cmake
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.31)
project(Sketchbook VERSION 0.1.0 LANGUAGES CXX)

find_package(Qt6 6.12 REQUIRED COMPONENTS Quick)
qt_standard_project_setup(REQUIRES 6.12
    I18N_SOURCE_LANGUAGE en
    I18N_TRANSLATED_LANGUAGES de es
)

qt_add_executable(app main.cpp)
qt_add_qml_module(app
    URI App
    QML_FILES Main.qml
    SOURCES AppController.cpp AppController.hpp
)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE Qt::Quick)
```

- `find_package()` locates Qt and the requested modules. Linking `Qt::Quick` gives the target
  the usage requirements for Qt Quick.
- `qt_standard_project_setup()` enables Qt's usual defaults, including automatic `moc` and
  `uic` processing for targets created afterwards if those settings are not already defined.
  `REQUIRES 6.12` rejects older Qt versions
  and opts in to Qt CMake policies through 6.12, so newer Qt releases do not silently change
  those policy choices. The language options describe the translation languages.
- `qt_add_executable()` creates an application target with Qt's platform-specific handling.
  `qt_add_qml_module()` then groups a module's URI, QML files, and C++ types and generates
  resources and tooling information. See @sec-qml-modules for how that module reaches a view.

In the template, `qt_standard_project_setup()` is in the top-level `CMakeLists.txt`,
`qt_add_executable()` is in `src/app/CMakeLists.txt`, and each feature has its own QML
module. The static modules and their plugins are linked into the application.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `CMakeLists.txt`, `src/app/CMakeLists.txt`, `src/canvas/CMakeLists.txt`

**Read more:** [Qt standard project setup](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qt-standard-project-setup.html),
[Qt executable targets](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qt-add-executable.html), and
[QML modules with CMake](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qt-add-qml-module.html).
:::

## One quality gate {#sec-build-checks}

Run tests during development and all checks before review:

```sh
cmake --workflow --preset dev
cmake --build --preset dev --target check
```

The first command compiles and tests. The second runs formatting, static checks, QML checks,
and license validation. CI repeats them on supported platforms.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `CMakePresets.json` and `.github/workflows/ci.yml`

**Read more:** [CMake presets](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/manual/cmake-presets.7.html).
:::
